title: Chirurgie des surfaces conformes : notes manuscrites (s.d., 1983-1984), lettres (1984).

deep.reconstruction:
The page is written upside down. Most of it is drawings for the 'surgery of conformal surfaces' project: spheres and discs with arcs, a ball divided by meridians, a long tube or cylinder decomposed into pieces, Y-shaped (pants-like) junctions, a disc on a stalk, hatched strips and a horizontal 'boundary' line. The drawings show a surface being cut along curves or graphs and reassembled.

The text is a short combinatorial definition. It supports the setting of the previous page, where moduli are studied for a configuration S ⊂ K ⊂ X: X is a compact oriented surface and K is an embedded cell complex or graph. The aim is to cut a cell complex K open along a subcomplex L.

1. View K as a poset of (closed) cells. For a cell x, set K_x = {y ∈ K | y ≤ x}, the closed cell with all its faces.
2. Define the cut complex as a colimit over the cells not in L: K̃ = colim_{x ∈ K∖L} K_x.
3. There is a canonical map π: K̃ → K.
4. Set L̃ = π⁻¹(L), with the induced map L̃ → L. On vertices this reads L̃_0 = π⁻¹(L_0) ⊂ K̃_0.

The stated properties are:
- π is an isomorphism away from L: |K̃| − |L̃| ≅ |K| − |L|.
- The pair (K̃, L̃) is 'pure'. Presumably this means every cell of L̃ lies in the closure of cells not in L̃, so K̃ − L̃ is dense and L̃ behaves like a boundary.

Cells of L are thereby duplicated, once for each local 'side' (each component of the local complement). This is the standard way of cutting a surface along a graph. In the dessins/surgery context, cutting X along K (or K along L) yields the faces f ∈ π_0(X−K) as surfaces with boundary. The next page counts moduli as a sum over these faces f, using terms of the form 3g(f) − 3 + (3/2)ν(f).

The line M(X_·, X_·) = [K̃_·] apparently records that a morphism or gluing datum between pieces is encoded by the class of the cut complex. It is too fragmentary to reconstruct with confidence.
errors: For π to be surjective (so that K̃ really is K cut open), every cell of L must be a face of some cell not in L. This holds exactly when K − L is dense in K, an implicit hypothesis that is not written.

The colimit has to be taken in a suitable category (posets, or regular CW complexes) and the K_x must be closed cells, i.e. K must be regular. Otherwise the gluing of duplicated faces is ill-defined. Not stated, but standard.

ideas.what: Cutting a (regular) cell complex K open along a subcomplex L, defined as the colimit of closed cells over the poset K∖L. Comes with π: K̃ → K, which is an isomorphism off L, and L̃ = π⁻¹(L) as the new 'boundary'.
ideas.modern_name: cutting/splitting along a subcomplex; unfolding or normalization of a stratified space; colimit-of-cells presentation of a regular CW poset
ideas.usually_credited_to: folklore of PL topology and combinatorial topology (e.g. cutting surfaces along curves in classical surface topology)
ideas.where_published: Not as such. The same viewpoint of a cell complex as a poset of cells underlies the combinatorial maps of Esquisse d'un programme (1984).

ideas.what: Pictorial program of conformal surgery: decomposing surfaces into discs, tubes and pants and regluing.
ideas.modern_name: pants decompositions / surgery of Riemann surfaces; plumbing
ideas.where_published: Esquisse d'un programme discusses Teichmüller towers and the role of pants and tori in a related way.

deep.surprise_reason: The page is a routine combinatorial definition (cutting a cell complex along a subcomplex via a colimit of closed cells) plus heuristic drawings. It is technical scaffolding for the moduli count on the next page and contains nothing absent from the literature.
transcription_corrections: Page is rotated 180°; the formulas read upside down.
'$\widetilde{L} = T$' is doubtful; it is probably part of '$\widetilde{L} = \pi^{-1}(L) \to L$' or a fragment of it, written near the top-right edge of the formula block.
'$M(X_i, X_j) = [\widetilde{K}_i]$': the indices are dots or placeholders (X_·, X_·, K̃_·), not clearly i, j.
The second formula line likely reads '$|\widetilde{K}| - |\widetilde{L}| \simeq |K| - |L|$', i.e. a difference of geometric realizations.
